h1: What Simla, Colorado Wells Really Cost and Produce
intro_html:
Buying rural property near Simla means evaluating more than a well permit. Records within five miles show a median completed depth of 218 feet, a median reported yield of 10.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 138 feet. Those figures are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for a particular lot.

The local record includes wells near Ramah and Matheson, with permits reaching back to the 1950s and the newest permit issued in 2025. Simla wells are entirely associated with Denver Basin aquifers, including Arapahoe, Laramie Fox Hills, and unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. A site-specific well permit review and neighboring-well check should be part of any purchase decision.

sections.heading: Simla well depths vary widely across the Denver Basin
sections.html:
The median reported depth near Simla is 218 feet. The middle half of wells falls from 65 to 374 feet, so a driller bidding a new well should not treat the median as a fixed target. About 34% of wells are under 100 feet, 26% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 35% are between 300 and 600 feet. Another 6% reach 600 feet or more.

The deepest recorded well is 960 feet. That spread reflects changing geology, the aquifer selected, and the location of the lot. Permits name Arapahoe in 150 wells and Laramie Fox Hills in 52. Unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers appear on 230 permits. Ask for nearby completed wells, not just a countywide average, before accepting a drilling estimate.

sections.heading: Expected well yield around Simla
sections.html:
Among the records reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 7.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute, giving a reasonable planning range for many properties. The yield mix is also favorable: 59% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, 25% report more than 15, and 17% report between 1 and 5.

No recorded wells in this dataset are under 1 gallon per minute, but that does not promise a result on an untested lot. A production test matters, especially where fractured rock is involved because fractures can make water output unpredictable. Confirm the permitted use as well. Domestic or household use appears on 51% of permits, stock use on 54%, and irrigation on 8%.

sections.heading: What the water levels show near Simla
sections.html:
Only 24 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. For those records, the median depth to water is 138 feet, with the middle half from 45 to 190 feet. That information helps a contractor think about pump setting, casing, and initial site planning, but it is not a full groundwater trend analysis for Simla.

The permit counts by decade do not establish that the water table is dropping. They show activity concentrated in the 1990s and 2000s, followed by fewer permits in the 2010s and 2020s. A buyer should obtain the actual static level and pumping information for nearby wells, then compare it with the proposed well location and aquifer. A Colorado Division of Water Resources permit does not guarantee a specific water level or yield.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Simla, and when
sections.html:
Permit records show steady well construction activity near Simla over many decades. There are 11 permits from the 1950s, 13 from the 1960s, 35 from the 1970s, 50 from the 1980s, 110 from the 1990s, 105 from the 2000s, 55 from the 2010s, and 38 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

Hamacher Well Works Inc, also listed as Hamacher, Alan Ray, appears most often, with 240 records. Can America Drilling, Inc., also listed as Arde, Wayne A., appears on 42. Authorized, including Pe and Pg entries, appears on 17. These records help identify local drilling history, but they are not endorsements. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scope, casing and grout specifications, pump testing, and the exact permit before hiring a driller.

sections.heading: Simla well drilling cost at local depths
sections.html:
The cost model for Simla assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the local median depth of 218 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at $10,900 to $15,300. That is only the hole, not a ready-to-use water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $16,900 to $27,300 at the median depth. A property needing a deeper hole can exceed that range, particularly because the local record includes wells as deep as 960 feet. Get a written bid that separates drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit-related work. A shallow estimate may not be comparable to a complete installation.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying a Simla lot
sections.html:
Low yield is not the leading pattern in the available records, but reported results still vary from 1 to 5 gallons per minute through more than 15 gallons per minute. Dry holes and poor production remain site-specific risks, particularly where fractured-bedrock conditions affect water storage and flow. Do not rely on a nearby well's yield without checking its distance, depth, aquifer, and use.

Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are 0 historic mine features in the mapped data. Ask for current water testing and review the location of the well relative to septic systems, drainfields, agricultural activity, and any environmental site. Building plans also need room for the well, septic system, access, utility trenching, and required separation areas.

sections.heading: A practical plan for building near Simla
sections.html:
Before closing, request the DWR permit and construction record for the subject well, then compare it with neighboring wells toward Ramah, Matheson, and other nearby areas. Focus on actual depth, static water level, pump yield, casing and grout, and the permitted use. If the property has no well, ask a licensed driller for a location-specific estimate rather than using the 218-foot median alone.

For a new home, confirm that the proposed household use is allowed by the permit. An exempt household-use well generally has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, while water rights and augmentation requirements can be important in over-appropriated basins. Coordinate the well location with septic, driveway, foundation, and electrical work before excavation starts. A production test and laboratory water test are sensible conditions of purchase or construction planning.

faq.q: What does a well produce near Simla?

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Simla?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 218-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $10,900 to $15,300. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $16,900 to $27,300. Deeper drilling can cost more, and the bid should state what is included.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Simla, Colorado?

Test the property's water through a qualified laboratory and review the well's location relative to septic systems, agriculture, and environmental sites before drinking it.
